steps.body:
Welcome back. Last time you made the console talk and listen. Quick warm-up before we build on it: remember that input() always hands you back text, and int() turns a string of digits into a real number. Good. Onward.

Right now your programs forget everything the instant they compute it. A variable fixes that. A variable is just a labeled box: you put a value in it and stick a name on the front, and later you can grab it by name.

You make one with a single equals sign: score = 10 means put 10 into a box and label it score. From then on, wherever you write score, Python reads the value inside. The equals sign here is not the one from math class asking is this equal. It is an arrow pointing left: take the thing on the right, drop it in the box on the left.

steps.prompt: Run this. Notice how the box can be refilled with a new value.
The middle line reads the box, adds 5, and puts the result back in the same box. What prints?

reviewForm.prompt: Which character assigns a value to a variable, as in count ___ 7 ?

steps.body:
Python does math the way you would expect, with a couple of extra tools worth knowing.

The usual crew: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide. One surprise: plain / always gives you a decimal, so 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5. A number with a decimal point is called a float; a whole number is an int.

Three power tools you will actually use:
** raises to a power, so 2 ** 3 is 8 (two, three times over).
// divides and throws away the remainder, so 17 // 5 is 3.
% gives you just the remainder, so 17 % 5 is 2. That percent sign is oddly useful: it is how you check if a number is even (n % 2 is 0) or wrap a value around a limit.

steps.body:
Back in Module 1 you glued text and values together with +, and you had to remember str() every time a number showed up. There is a much nicer way.

An f-string is a sentence with slots. Put a letter f right before the opening quote, then drop any value straight into the text inside curly braces. Python fills each slot in for you.

Instead of "You scored " + str(points) + " points", you write f"You scored {points} points". Same result, far less fuss, and it even does math inside the braces: f"double is {points * 2}". Once you meet f-strings you rarely go back to gluing with +.

steps.prompt: Run this. The values drop right into the slots.
The braces can hold a little math too. What prints?
steps.code:
x = 5
print(f"x is {x} and double is {x * 2}")

reviewForm.code:

print(f"x is {x} and double is {x * 2}")

steps.body:
Some values are not text or numbers. They are answers to a yes-or-no question, and there are only two of them: True and False. Python calls this kind of value a boolean.

You rarely type True yourself. You get booleans by ASKING questions with comparisons: 10 > 3 gives True, 3 > 5 gives False. Note the double equals for is this equal: 7 == 7 is True. Single = fills a box; double == asks a question. Mixing those two up is a classic early bug, so it is worth burning in now.

When you are not sure what kind of value you are holding, type() will tell you. type("hi") reports it is a str, type(5) reports an int. You will lean on booleans hard next module, when your programs start making decisions.

steps.prompt: A comparison produces a boolean. What prints?
What KIND of value is "hello" (with the quotes)?

steps.body:
Time to put variables, math, and f-strings to work on something with a real shape. No new ideas here, just combining what you have.

One handy tool for money math: round(value, 2) trims a number to two decimal places, so round(108.0, 2) stays 108.0 and round(17.519, 2) becomes 17.52. You will want that any time you are dealing with dollars.

steps.prompt: Fill in with_tax so it takes a price and a tax percent and returns the price with tax added, rounded to two decimals. Example: with_tax(100, 8) returns 108.0 (8 percent of 100 is 8). The def line is provided; just write the return.

hiddenTests.message: with_tax(100, 8) should be 108.0 (add 8 percent of the price)
check 0 percent tax: with_tax(20, 0) should be 20.0, unchanged

hints: A percent is out of 100, so 8 percent is tax_percent / 100.
Adding that percent means multiplying by (1 + tax_percent / 100).
steps.modelSolution:
def with_tax(price, tax_percent):
    return round(price * (1 + tax_percent / 100), 2)

reviewForm.prompt: Fill the blank to add a percent: price * (1 ___ tax_percent / 100)

boss.name: The Tab Splitter
boss.taunt: Four friends, one bill, and a tip. Make the numbers come out fair.
boss.brief:
Dinner is done and the check lands on the table. Write the function that settles it fairly.

Fill in split_bill(bill, tip_percent, people) so it returns what EACH person pays: take the bill, add the tip, divide by the number of people, and round to two decimals.

Worked example with real numbers: split_bill(58.40, 20, 4) should return 17.52. Here is why: 20 percent of 58.40 is a tip, giving a total of 70.08, split four ways is 17.52 each.

terms.definition: A labeled box that holds a value. You make one with =, as in score = 10, and read it back by name.
A number with a decimal point, like 5.0 or 17.52. Plain division always gives you a float.
The remainder after division. 17 % 5 is 2. Handy for checking even or odd and for wrapping values around a limit.
A sentence with slots. Put f before the quote and drop values into {curly braces}: f"You scored {points} points".
A yes-or-no value, either True or False. You usually get one by asking a question, like 10 > 3.
One equals sign fills a box (assignment). Two equals signs ask is this equal (a comparison that gives True or False). Mixing them up is a classic early bug.
